div.head: TO THE RIGHT HONORABLE RALPH; EARL OF MONTAGUE, &c.
div.p:
My Lord,
Whether the world will arraign me of vanity or not, that
I have presumed to dedicate this comedy to your Lordship,
I am yet in doubt, though it may be it is some degree of
vanity even to doubt of it. One who has at any time had
the honor of your Lordship’s conversation, cannot be
supposed to think very meanly of that which he would prefer
to your perusal; yet it were to incur the imputation of too
much sufficiency, to pretend to such a merit as might abide
the test of your Lordship’s censure.
Whatever value may be wanting to this play while yet it
is mine, will be sufficiently made up to it when it is once
become your Lordship’s; and it is my security that I cannot
have overrated it more by my dedication than your Lordship
will dignify it by your patronage.
That it succeeded on the stage was almost beyond my
expectation; for but little of it was prepared for that general
taste which seems now to be predominant in the palates of
our audience.
Those characters which are meant to be ridiculous in most
of our comedies are of fools so gross that, in my humble
opinion, they should rather disturb than divert the well-natured
and reflecting part of an audience; they are rather
objects of charity than contempt; and instead of moving our
mirth, they ought very often to excite our compassion.
This reflection moved me to design some characters which
should appear ridiculous, not so much through a natural
folly (which is incorrigible, and therefore not proper for
the stage) as through an affected wit; a wit, which, at the
same time that it is affected, is also false. As there is some
difficulty in the formation of a character of this nature, so
there is some hazard which attends the progress of its
success upon the stage; for many come to a play so over-charged
with criticism that they very often let fly their
censure, when through their rashness they have mistaken
their aim. This I had occasion lately to observe; for this
play had been acted two or three days before some of these
hasty judges could find the leisure to distinguish betwixt the
character of a Witwoud and a Truewit.
I must beg your Lordship’s pardon for this digression
from the true course of this epistle; but that it may not
seem altogether impertinent, I beg that I may plead the
occasion of it, in part of that excuse of which I stand in need,
for recommending this comedy to your protection. It is
only by the countenance of your Lordship, and the few so
qualified, that such who write with care and pains can hope
to be distinguished; for the prostituted name of poet promiscuously
levels all that bear it.
Terence, the most correct writer in the world, had a
Scipio and a Laelius, if not to assist him, at least to support
him in his reputation; and notwithstanding his extra-
ordinary merit, it may be their countenance was not more
than necessary.
The purity of his style, the delicacy of his turns, and the
justness of his characters were all of them beauties which the
greater part of his audience were incapable of tasting; some
of the coarsest strokes of Plautus, so severely censured by
Horace, were more likely to affect the multitude, such who
come with expectation to laugh out the last act of a play,
and are better entertained with two or three unseasonable
jests than with the artful solution of the fable.
As Terence excelled in his performances, so had he great
advantages to encourage his undertakings, for he built most
on the foundations of Menander; his plots were generally
modeled, and his characters ready drawn to his hand. He
copied Menander, and Menander had no less light in the
formation of his characters from the observations of Theophrastus,
of whom he was a disciple, but the immediate successor
of Aristotle, the first and greatest judge of poetry. These
were great models to design by; and the further advantage
which Terence possessed, towards giving his plays the due
ornaments of purity of style and justness of manners, was
not less considerable from the freedom of conversation which
was permitted him with Laelius and Scipio, two of the greatest
and most polite men of his age. And indeed the privilege
of such a conversation is the only certain means of attaining
to the perfection of dialogue.
If it has happened in any part of this comedy that I have
gained a turn of style or expression more correct, or at least
more corrigible, than in those which I have formerly
written, I must, with equal pride and gratitude, ascribe it
to the honor of your Lordship’s admitting me into your
conversation, and that of a society where everybody else was
so well worthy of you, in your retirement last summer from
the town; for it was immediately after that this comedy was
written. If I have failed in my performance, it is only to be
regretted, where there were so many not inferior either to a
Scipio or a Laelius, that there should be one wanting equal
to the capacity of a Terence.
If I am not mistaken, poetry is almost the only art which
has not yet laid claim to your Lordship’s patronage. Architecture
and painting, to the great honor of our country,
have flourished under your influence and protection. In the
meantime, poetry, the eldest sister of all arts, and parent
of most, seems to have resigned her birthday, by having
neglected to pay her duty to your Lordship, and by permitting
others of a later extraction to prepossess that place in
your esteem to which none can pretend a better title. Poetry,
in its nature, is sacred to the good and great; the relation
between them is reciprocal, and they are ever propitious to
it. It is the privilege of poetry to address to them, and it is
their prerogative alone to give it protection.
This received maxim is a general apology for all writers
who consecrate their labors to great men; but I could wish
at this time that this address were exempted from the
common pretense of all dedications; and that, as I can
distinguish your Lordship even among the most deserving, so
this offering might become remarkable by some particular
instance of respect, which should assure your Lordship that I
am, with all due sense of your extreme worthiness and
humanity,
My Lord,
Your Lordship’s most obedient
and most obliged humble servant
Will. Congreve

div1.head: [I]
div1.stage: Mirabell and Fainall, rising from cards; Betty waiting.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: You are a fortunate man, Mr. Fainall.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Have we done?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: What you please. I’ll play on to entertain you.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
No, I’ll give you your revenge another time, when you are
not so indifferent; you are thinking of something else now,
and play too negligently. The coldness of a losing gamester
lessens the pleasure of the winner. I’d no more play with a
man that slighted his ill fortune than I’d make love to a
woman who undervalued the loss of her reputation.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You have a taste extremely delicate and are for refining on
your pleasures.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Prithee, why so reserved? Something has put you out of
humor.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Not at all; I happen to be grave today, and you are gay;
that’s all.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Confess, Millamant and you quarreled last night, after I
left you; my fair cousin has some humors that would tempt
the patience of a stoic. What, some coxcomb came in, and
was well received by her, while you were by.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Witwoud and Petulant, and what was worse, her aunt, your
wife’s mother, my evil genius; or to sum up all in her own
name, my old Lady Wishfort came in.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Oh, there it is then! She has a lasting passion for you, and
with reason. What, then my wife was there?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Yes, and Mrs. Marwood and three or four more, whom I
never saw before. Seeing me, they all put on their grave
faces, whispered one another; then complained aloud of the
vapors, and after fell into a profound silence.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: They had a mind to be rid of you.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
For which reason I resolved not to stir. At last the good old
lady broke through her painful taciturnity, with an invective
against long visits. I would not have understood her, but
Millamant joining in the argument, I rose and with a con-
strained smile told her, I though nothing was so easy as to
know when a visit began to be troublesome. She reddened
and I withdrew, without expecting her reply.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
You were to blame to resent what she spoke only in com-
pliance with her aunt.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
She is more mistress of herself than to be under the
necessity of such a resignation.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
What? though half her fortune depends upon her marrying
with my lady’s approbation?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I was then in such a humor, that I should have been better
pleased if she had been less discreet.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Now I remember, I wonder not they were weary of you.
Last night was one of their cabal-nights; they have ’em three
times a week, and meet by turns, at one another’s apart-
ments, where they come together like the coroner’s inquest,
to sit upon the murdered reputation of the week. You and
I are excluded; and it was once proposed that all the male
sex should be excepted; but somebody moved that, to
avoid scandal, there might be one man of the community;
upon which motion Witwoud and Petulant were enrolled
members.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
And who may have been the foundress of this sect? My
Lady Wishfort, I warrant, who published her detestation
of mankind, and full of the vigor of fifty-five, declares for
a friend and ratafia; and let posterity shift for itself, she’ll
breed no more.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
The discovery of your sham addresses to her, to conceal
your love to her niece, has provoked this separation. Had
you dissembled better, things might have continued in the
state of nature.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I did as much as man could, with any reasonable con-
science. I proceeded to the very last act of flattery with her,
and was guilty of a song in her commendation. Nay, I got
a friend to put her into a lampoon, and compliment her
with the imputation of an affair with a young fellow, which
I carried so far, that I told her the malicious town took
notice that she was grown fat of a sudden; and when she lay
in of a dropsy, persuaded her she was reported to be in
labor. The devil’s in’t, if an old woman is to be flattered
further, unless a man should endeavor downright personally
to debauch her; and that my virtue forbade me. But for the
discovery of that amour, I am indebted to your friend, or
your wife’s friend, Mrs. Marwood.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
What should provoke her to be your enemy, unless she has
made you advances, which you have slighted? Women do
not easily forgive omissions of that nature.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
She was always civil to me, till of late. I confess I am not
one of those coxcombs who are apt to interpret a woman’s
good manners to her prejudice, and think that she who does
not refuse ’em everything can refuse ’em nothing.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
You are a gallant man, Mirabell; and though you may
have cruelty enough not to satisfy a lady’s longing, you have
too much generosity not to be tender of her honor. Yet you
speak with an indifference which seems to be affected, and
confesses you are conscious of a negligence.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You pursue the argument with a distrust that seems to be
unaffected, and confesses you are conscious of a concern for
which the lady is more indebted to you than your wife.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Fie, fie, friend! If you grow censorious, I must leave you.
I’ll look upon the gamesters in the next room.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Who are they?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Petulant and Witwoud. [To Betty.] Bring me some
chocolate.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Betty, what says your clock?

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: Turned of the last canonical hour, sir.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
How pertinently the jade answers me! (Looking on his watch.)
Ha? almost one o’clock! Oh, y’are come! Enter a Servant.
Well, is the grand affair over? You have been something
tedious.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p:
Sir, there’s such coupling at Pancras, that they stand behind
one another, as ’twere in a county dance. Ours was the
last couple to lead up; and no hopes appearing of dispatch,
besides the parson growing hoarse, we were afraid his lungs
would have failed before it came to our turn; so we drove
round to Duke’s Place, and there they were riveted in a
trice.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: So, so, you are sure they are married.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Married and bedded, sir; I am witness.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Have you the certificate?

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Here it is, sir.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Has the tailor brought Waitwell’s clothes home, and the
new liveries?

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
That’s well. Do you go home again, d’ye hear, and adjourn
the consummation till father order; bid Waitwell shake his
ears, and Dame Partlet rustle up her feathers, and meet me at
one o’clock by Rosamond’s Pond, that I may see her before
she returns to her lady; and as you tender your ears, be
secret.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Joy of your success, Mirabell; you look pleased.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Aye, I have been engaged in a matter of some sort of mirth,
which is not yet ripe for discovery. I am glad this is not a
cabal-night. I wonder, Fainall, that you who are married,
and of consequence should be discreet, will suffer your wife
to be of such a party.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Faith, I am not jealous. Besides, most who are engaged are
women and relations; and for the men, they are of a kind
too contemptible to give scandal.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I am of another opinion. The greater the coxcomb, always
the more scandal; for a woman who is not a fool can have
but one reason for associating with a man that is.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Are you jealous as often as you see Witwoud entertained by
Millamant?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Of her understanding I am, if not of her person.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: You do her wrong; for, to give her her due, she has wit.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
She has beauty enough to make any man think so, and com-
plaisance enough not to contradict him who shall tell her so.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
For a passionate lover, methinks you are a man somewhat
too discerning in the failings of your mistress.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
And for a discerning man, somewhat too passionate a lover;
for I like her with all her faults; nay, like her for her faults.
Her follies are so natural, or so artful, that they become her;
and those affectations which in another woman would be
odious, serve but to make her more agreeable. I’ll tell thee,
Fainall, she once used me with that insolence, that in
revenge I took her to pieces; sifted her and separated her
failings; I studied ’em, and got ’em by rote. The catalogue
was so large that I was not without hopes one day or other
to hate her heartily: to which end I so used myself to think
of ’em that at length, contrary to my design and expectation,
they gave me every hour less and less disturbance; till in a
few days it became habitual to me to remember ’em without
being displeased. They are now grown as familiar to me as
my own frailties; and in all probability, in a little time
longer I shall like ’em as well.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Marry her, marry her! Be half as well acquainted with
her charms as you are with her defects, and my life on’t, you
are your own man again.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Say you so?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Aye, aye, I have experience: I have a wife, and so forth.

sp.speaker: MESSENGER.
sp.p: Is one Squire Witwoud here?

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: Yes; what’s your business?

sp.speaker: MESSENGER.
sp.p:
I have a letter for him, from his brother Sir Wilfull, which
I am charged to deliver into his own hands.

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: He’s in the next room, friend; that way.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
What, is the chief of that noble family in town, Sir Wilfull
Witwoud?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: He is expected today. Do you know him?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I have seen him. He promises to be an extraordinary
person; I think you have the honor to be related to him.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Yes, he is half brother to this Witwoud by a former wife,
who was sister to my Lady Wishfort, my wife’s mother. If
you marry Millamant, you must call cousins too.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: I had rather be his relation than his acquaintance.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: He comes to town in order to equip himself for travel.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: For travel! Why the man I mean is above forty.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
No matter for that; ’tis for the honor of England that all
Europe should know we have blockheads of all ages.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I wonder there is not an act of parliament to save the
credit of the nation, and prohibit the exportation of fools.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
By no means; ’tis better as ’tis. ’tis better to trade with a
little loss, than to be quite eaten up with being over-
stocked.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Pray, are the follies of this knight-errant and those of the
squire his brother anything related?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Not at all; Witwoud grows by the knight, like a medlar
grafted on a crab. One will melt in your mouth, and t’other
set your teeth on edge; one is all pulp, and the other all core.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
So one will be rotten before he be ripe, and the other will be
rotten without ever being ripe at all.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Sir Wilfull is an odd mixture of bashfulness and obstinacy.
But when he’s drunk, he’s as loving as the monster in The
Tempest, and much after the same manner. To give t’other
his due, he has something of good nature and does not always
want wit.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Not always; but as often as his memory fails him, and his
commonplace of comparison. He is a fool with a good
memory and some few scraps of other folks’ wit. He is one
whose conversation can never be approved, yet it is now
and then to be endured. He has indeed one good quality, he
is not exceptious; for he so passionately affects the reputation
of understanding raillery, that he will construe an affront
into a jest, and call downright rudeness and ill language
satire and fire.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
If you have a mind to finish his picture, you have an opportunity
to do it full length. Behold the original!

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Afford me your compassion, my dears! Pity me, Fainall!
Mirabell, pity me!

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: I do from my soul.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Why, what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: No letters for me, Betty?

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: Did not the messenger bring you one but now, sir?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: Aye, but no other?

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: No, sir.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
That’s hard, that’s very hard. A messenger, a mule, a beast
of burden! He has brought me a letter from the fool my
brother, as heavy as a panegyric in a funeral sermon, or a
copy of commendatory verses from one poet to another.
And what’s worse, ’tis as sure a forerunner of the author as
an epistle dedicatory.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: A fool, and your brother Witwoud!

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Aye, aye, my half brother. My half brother he is, no nearer
upon honor.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Then ’tis possible he may be but half a fool.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Good, good, Mirabell, le drôle! Good, good; hang him,
don’t let’s talk of him. Fainall, how does your lady? Gad, I
say anything in the world to get this fellow out of my head.
I beg pardon that I should ask a man of pleasure, and the
town, a question at once so foreign and domestic. But I talk
like an old maid at a marriage, I don’t know what I say; but
she’s the best woman in the world.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
’Tis well you don’t know what you say, or else your
commendation would go near to make me either vain or
jealous.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
No man in town lives well with a wife but Fainall. Your
judgment, Mirabell.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You had better step and ask his wife, if you would be
credibly informed.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: Mirabell.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Aye.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
My dear, I ask ten thousand pardons. Gad, I have forgot
what I was going to say to you!

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: I thank you heartily, heartily.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: No, but prithee excuse me: my memory is such a memory.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Have a care of such apologies, Witwoud; for I never knew
a fool but he affected to complain, either of the spleen or his
memory.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: What have you done with Petulant?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
He’s reckoning his money, my money it was. I have no
luck today.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
You may allow him to win of you at play, for you are sure
to be too hard for him at repartee; since you monopolize the
wit that is between you, the fortune must be his of course.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I don’t find that Petulant confesses the superiority of wit
to be your talent, Witwoud.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Come, come, you are malicious now, and would breed
debates. Petulant’s my friend, and a very honest fellow, and
a very pretty fellow, and has a smattering—faith and troth,
a pretty deal of an odd sort of a small wit: nay, I’ll do him
justice. I’m his friend, I won’t wrong him neither. And if
he had but any judgment in the world, he would not be
altogether contemptible. Come, come, don’t detract from
the merits of my friend.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: You don’t take your friend to be over-nicely bred?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
No, no, hang him, the rogue has no manners at all, that
I must own. No more breeding than a bum-baily, that I
grant you. ’Tis pity, faith; the fellow has fire and life.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: What, courage?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Hum, faith, I don’t know as to that, I can’t say as to that.
Yes, faith, in a controversy he’ll contradict anybody.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Though ’twere a man whom he feared, or a woman whom
he loved.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Well, well, he does not always think before he speaks; we
have all our failing. You’re too hard upon him, you are,
faith. Let me excuse him. I can defend most of his faults,
except one or two. One he has, that’s the truth on’t; if he
were my brother, I could not acquit him. That, indeed, I
could wish were otherwise.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Aye, marry, what’s that, Witwoud?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Oh, pardon me! Expose the infirmities of my friend! No, my
dear, excuse me there.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: What, I warrant he’s unsincere, or ’tis some such trifle.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
No, no, what if he be? ’Tis no matter for that, his wit will
excuse that. A wit should no more be sincere than a
woman constant; one argues a decay of parts, as t’other of
beauty.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Maybe you think him too positive?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
No, no, his being positive is an incentive to argument, and
keeps up conversation.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Too illiterate?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
That! that’s his happiness; his want of learning gives him
the more opportunities to show his natural parts.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: He wants words?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Aye, but I like him for that now; for his want of words
gives me the pleasure very often to explain his meaning.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: He’s imprudent?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: No, that’s not it.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Vain?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
What! he speaks unseasonable truths sometimes, because he
has not wit enough to invent an evasion?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Truths! ha! ha! ha! No, no, since you will have it, I mean he
never speaks truth at all, that’s all. He will lie like a chamber-
maid, or a woman of quality’s porter. Now that is a fault.

sp.speaker: COACHMAN.
sp.p: Is Master Petulant here, mistress?

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: COACHMAN.
sp.p: Three gentlewomen in the coach would speak with him.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Oh brave Petulant! Three!

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: I’ll tell him.

sp.speaker: COACHMAN.
sp.p:
You must bring two dishes of chocolate and a glass of
cinnamon-water.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
That should be for two fasting strumpets, and a bawd
troubled with wind. Now you may know what the three
are.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: You are very free with your friend’s acquaintance.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Aye, aye, friendship without freedom is as dull as love
without enjoyment, or wine without toasting; but to tell
you a secret, these are trulls that he allows coach-hire,
and something more, by the week, to call on him once a day
at public places.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
You shall see he won’t go to ’em because there’s no more
company here to take notice of him. Why, this is nothing to
what he used to do: before he found out this way, I have
know him call for himself.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Call for himself? What dost thou mean?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Mean! Why, he would slip you out of this chocolate-house,
just when you had been talking to him. As soon as your
back was turned, whip, he was gone! Then trip to his lodging,
clap on a hood and scarf, and mask, slap into a hackney-
coach, and drive hither to the door again in a trice, where
he would send in for himself; that I mean, call for himself,
wait for himself; nay, and what’s more, not finding himself,
sometimes leave a letter for himself.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I confess this is something extraordinary. I believe he waits
for himself now, he is so long a-coming. Oh! I ask his pardon.

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: Sir, the coach stays.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Well, well; I come. ’Sbud, a man had as good be a professed
midwife as a professed whoremaster, at this rate! To be
knocked up and raised at all hours, and in all places! Pox
on ’em, I won’t come! D’ye hear, tell ’em I won’t come.
Let ’em snivel and cry their hearts out.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: You are very cruel, Petulant.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: All’s one, let it pass. I have a humor to be cruel.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I hope they are not persons of condition that you use at this
rate.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Condition! Condition’s a dried fig, if I am not in humor!
By this hand, if they were your—a—a—your what-d’ye-call-’ems
themselves, they must wait or rub off, if I want
appetite.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: What-d’ye-call-’ems! What are they, Witwoud?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Empresses, my dear; by your what-d’ye-call-’ems he means
sultana queens.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: Aye, Roxolanas.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Cry you mercy.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Witwoud says they are—

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: What does he say th’are?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: I? Fine ladies, I say.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Pass on, Witwoud. Harkee, by this light his relations: two
co-heiresses his cousins, and an old aunt, that loves caterwauling
better than a conventicle.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Ha! ha! ha! I had a mind to see how the rogue would
come off. Ha! ha! ha! Gad, I can’t be angry with him, if he
had said they were my mother and my sisters.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
No; the rogue’s wit and readiness of invention charm me.
Dear Petulant!

sp.speaker: BETTY.
sp.p: They are gone, sir, in great anger.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Enough, let ’em trundle. Anger helps complexion, saves
paint.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
This continence is all dissembled; this is in order to have
something to brag of the next time he makes court to
Millamant, and swear he has abandoned the whole sex
for her sake.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Have you not left off your imprudent pretensions there
yet? I shall cut your throat some time or other, Petulant,
about that business.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: Aye, aye, let that pass. There are other throats to be cut.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Meaning mine, sir?

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Not I. I mean nobody; I know nothing. But there are
uncles and nephews in the world, and they may be rivals.
What then? All’s one for that.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
How! Harkee Petulant, come hither. Explain, or I shall
call your interpreter.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Explain! I know nothing. Why, you have an uncle, have you
not, lately come to town, and lodges by my Lady Wishfort’s?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: True.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Why, that’s enough. You and he are not friends; and if he
should marry and have a child, you may be disinherited,
ha?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Where hast thou stumbled upon all this truth?

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: All’s one for that; why, then say I know something.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Come, thou art an honest fellow, Petulant, and shalt make
love to my mistress, thou sha’t, faith. What hast thou heard
of my uncle?

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
I? Nothing I. If throats are to be cut, let swords clash!
Snug’s the word; I shrug and am silent.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Oh, raillery, raillery! Come, I know thou art in the
women’s secrets. What, you’re a cabalist; I know you stayed
at Millamant’s last night, after I went. Was there any
mention made of my uncle or me? Tell me. If thou hadst
but good nature equal to thy wit, Petulant, Tony Witwoud,
who is now thy competitor in fame, would show as dim by
thee as a dead whiting’s eye by a pearl of orient; he would
no more be seen by thee than Mercury is by the sun. Come,
I’m sure thou wo’t tell me.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
If I do, will you grant me common sense then for the
future?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Faith, I’ll do what I can for thee; and I’ll pray that Heaven
may grant it thee in the meantime.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: Well, harkee.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Petulant and you both will find Mirabell as warm a rival as
a lover.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Pshaw! pshaw! That she laughs at Petulant is plain. And for
my part, but that it is almost a fashion to admire her, I
should—harkee, to tell you a secret, but let it go no further;
between friends, I shall never break my heart for her.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: She’s handsome; but she’s a sort of an uncertain woman.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: I thought you had died for her.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: Umh—no—

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: She has wit.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
’Tis what she will hardly allow anybody else. Now, demme,
I should hate that, if she were as handsome as Cleopatra.
Mirabell is not so sure of her as he thinks for.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Why do you think so?

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
We stayed pretty late there last night, and heard something
of an uncle to Mirabell, who is lately come to town, and
is between him and the best part of his estate. Mirabell and
he are at some distance, as my Lady Wishfort has been told;
and you know she hates Mirabell worse than a Quaker hates
a parrot, or than a fishmonger hates a hard frost. Whether
this uncle has seen Mrs. Millamant or not, I cannot say;
but there were items of such a treaty being in embryo, and
if it should come to life, poor Mirabell would be in some
sort unfortunately fobbed, i’faith.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: ’Tis impossible Millamant should hearken to it.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Faith, my dear, I can’t tell; she’s a woman and a kind of a
humorist.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: And is this the sum of what you could collect last night?

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
The quintessence. Maybe Witwoud knows more; he stayed
longer. Besides, they never mind him; they say anything
before him.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: I thought you had been the greatest favorite.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: Aye, tête à tête, but not in public, because I make remarks.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: You do?

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Aye, aye, pox, I’m malicious, man! Now he’s soft, you
know, they are not in awe of him. The fellow’s well-bred,
he’s what you call a —what-d’ye-call-’em, a fine gentleman,
but he’s silly withal.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I thank you. I know as much as my curiosity requires.
Fainall, are you for the Mall?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Aye, I’ll take a turn before dinner.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Aye, we’ll all walk in the park; the ladies talked of being
there.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I thought you were obligated to watch for your brother Sir
Wilfull’s arrival.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
No, no, he comes to his aunt’s, my Lady Wishfort. Pox on
him! I shall be troubled with him too; what shall I do with
the fool?

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Beg him for his estate, that I may beg you afterwards; and so
have but one trouble with you both.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Oh, rare Petulant! Thou art as quick as a fire in a frosty
morning; thou shalt to the Mall with us, and we’ll be
very severe.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p: Enough, I’m in a humor to be severe.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Are you? Pray then walk by yourselves. Let not us be
accessory to your putting the ladies out of countenance with
your senseless ribaldry, which you roar out aloud as often as
they pass by you; and when you have made a handsome
woman blush, then you think you have been severe.

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
What, what? Then let ’em show their innocence by not
understanding what they hear, or else show their discretion
by not hearing what they would not be thought to under-
stand.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
But hast not thou then sense enough to know that thou
ought’st to be most ashamed thyself, when thou hast put
another out of countenance?

sp.speaker: PETULANT.
sp.p:
Not I, by this hand! I always take blushing either for a sign
of guilt or ill-breeding.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I confess you ought to think so. You are in the right, that
you may plead the error of your judgment in defense of your
practice.
Where modesty’s ill manners, ’tis but fit
That imprudence and malice pass for wit.

div1.head: [II]
div1.stage: Enter Mrs. Fainall and Mrs. Marwood.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Aye, aye, dear Marwood, if we will be happy, we must
find the means in ourselves, and among ourselves. Men
are ever in extremes, either doting or averse. While they are
lovers, if they have fire and sense, their jealousies are insupportable.
And when they cease to love (we ought to
think at least) they loathe; they look upon us with horror
and distaste; they meet us like the ghosts of what we were,
and as such, fly from us.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
True, ’tis an unhappy circumstance of life, that love should
ever die before us; and that the man so often should outlive
the lover. But say what you will, ’tis better to be left than
never to have been loved. To pass our youth in dull indifference,
to refuse the sweets of life because they once must leave
us, is as preposterous as to wish to have been born old,
because we one day must be old. For my part, my youth
may wear and waste, but it shall never rust in my possession.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Then it seems you dissemble an aversion to mankind, only
in compliance with my mother’s humor.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Certainly. To be free, I have no taste of those insipid dry
discourses with which our sex of force must entertain them-
selves, apart from men. We may affect endearments to each
other, profess eternal friendships, and seem to dote like
lovers; but ’tis not in our natures long to persevere. Love will
resume his empire in our breasts; and every heart, or soon or
late, receive and readmit him as its lawful tyrant.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Bless me, how have I been deceived! Why you profess a
libertine!

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
You see my friendship by my freedom. Come, be as sincere,
acknowledge that your sentiments agree with mine.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Never!

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: You hate mankind?

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Heartily, inveterately.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Your husband?

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Most transcendently; aye, though I say it, meritoriously.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Give me your hand upon it.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: There.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: I join with you; what I have said has been to try you.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Is it possible? Dost thou hate those vipers, men?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
I have done hating ’em, and am now come to despise ’em;
the next thing I have to do, is eternally to forget ’em.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: There spoke the spirit of an Amazon, a Penthesilea.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
And yet I am thinking sometimes to carry my aversion
further.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Faith, by marrying; if I could but find one that loved me
very well and would be thoroughly sensible of ill usage, I
think I should do myself the violence of undergoing the
ceremony.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: You would not make him a cuckold?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: No, but I’d make him believe I did, and that’s as bad.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Why had not you as good do it?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Oh, if he should ever discover it, he would then know the
worst, and be out of his pain; but I would have him ever to
continue upon the rack of fear and jealousy.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Ingenious mischief! Would thou wert married to Mirabell.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Would I were!

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: You change color.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Because I hate him.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
So do I; but I can hear him named. But what reason have
you to hate him in particular?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
I never loved him; he is, and always was, insufferably
proud.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
By the reason you give for your aversion, one would think it
dissembled; for you have laid a fault to his charge of which his
enemies must acquit him.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Oh, then it seems you are one of his favorable enemies!
Methinks you look a little pale, and now you flush again.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Do I? I think I am a little sick o’ the sudden.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: What ails you?

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
My husband. Don’t you see him? He turned short upon me
unawares, and has almost overcome me.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! He comes opportunely for you.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: For you, for he has brought Mirabell with him.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: My dear!

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: My soul!

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: You don’t look well today, child.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: D’ye think so?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: He is the only man that does, madam.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
The only man that would tell me so at least; and the only
man from whom I could hear it without mortification.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Oh my dear, I am satisfied of your tenderness; I know you
cannot resent anything from me, especially what is an effect
of my concern.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Mr. Mirabell, my mother interrupted you in a pleasant
relation last night; I would fain hear it out.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
The persons concerned in that affair have yet a tolerable
reputation. I am afraid Mr. Fainall will be censorious.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
He has a humor more prevailing than his curiosity, and
will willingly dispense with the hearing of one scandalous
story, to avoid giving an occasion to make another by
being seen to walk with his wife. This way, Mr. Mirabell,
and I dare promise you will oblige us both.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Excellent creature! Well, sure if I should live to be rid of
my wife, I should be a miserable man.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Aye!

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
For having only that one hope, the accomplishment of it, of
consequence must put an end to all my hopes; and what a
wretch is he who must survive his hopes! Nothing remains
when that day comes, but to sit down and weep like Alexander,
when he wanted other worlds to conquer.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Will you not follow ’em?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Faith, I think not.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Pray let us; I have a reason.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: You are not jealous?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Of whom?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Of Mirabell.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
If I am, is it inconsistent with my love to you that I am
tender of your honor?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
You would intimate then, as if there were a fellow-feeling
between my wife and him.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
I think she does not hate him to that degree she would be
thought.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: But he, I fear, is too insensible.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: It may be you are deceived.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: It may be so. I do now begin to apprehend it.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: That I have been deceived, madam, and you are false.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: That I am false! What mean you?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
To let you know I see through all your little arts. Come,
you both love him; and both have equally dissembled your
aversion. Your mutual jealousies of one another have made
you clash till you have both struck fire. I have seen the warm
confession reddening on your cheeks, and sparkling from
your eyes.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: You do me wrong.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
I do not. ’Twas for my ease to oversee and willfully neglect
the gross advances made him by my wife; that by permitting
her to be engaged, I might continue unsuspected in my
pleasure, and take you oftener to my arms in full security.
But could you think, because the nodding husband would
not wake, that e’er the watchful lover slept?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: And wherewithal can you reproach me?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: With infidelity, with loving of another, with love of Mirabell.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
’Tis false. I challenge you to show an instance that can
confirm your groundless accusation. I hate him.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
And wherefore do you hate him? He is insensible, and your
resentment follows his neglect. An instance? The injuries
you have done him are a proof, you interposing in his love.
What cause had you to make discoveries of his pretended
passion? To undeceive the credulous aunt, and be the
officious obstacle of his match with Millamant?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
My obligations to my lady urged me; I had professed a
friendship to her, and could not see her easy nature so
abused by that dissembler.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
What, was it conscience then? Professed a friendship! Oh,
the pious friendships of the female sex!

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
More tender, more sincere, and more enduring, than all
the vain and empty vows of men, whether professing love
to us, or mutual faith to one another.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! you are my wife’s friend too.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Shame and ingratitude! Do you reproach me? You, you
upbraid me! Have I been false to her, though strict
fidelity to you, and sacrificed my friendship to keep my love
inviolate? And have you the baseness to charge me with the
guilt, unmindful of the merit! To you it should be merito-
rious, that I have been vicious; and do you reflect that
guilt upon me, which should lie buried in your bosom?

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
You misinterpret my reproof. I meant but to remind you of
the slight account you once could make of strictest ties, when
set in comparison with your love to me.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
’Tis false; you urged it with deliberate malice! ’Twas spoke
in scorn, and I never will forgive it.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Your guilt, not your resentment, begets your rage. If yet you
loved, you could forgive a jealousy; but you are stung to find
you are discovered.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
It shall be all discovered. You too shall be discovered; be
sure you shall. I can but de exposed. If I do it myself, I
shall prevent your baseness.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Why, what will you do?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Disclose it to your wife; own what has passed between us.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Frenzy!

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
By all my wrongs I’ll do’t? I’ll publish to the world the
injuries you have done me, both in my fame and fortune!
With both I trusted you, you bankrupt in honor, as indigent
of wealth.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Your fame I have preserved. Your fortune has been bestowed
as the prodigality of your love would have it, in
pleasures which we both have shared. Yet had not you been
false, I had ere this repaid it. ’Tis true, had you permitted
Mirabell with Millamant to have stolen their marriage, my
lady had been incensed beyond all means of reconcilement;
Millamant had forfeited the moiety of her fortune, which
then would have descended to my wife. And wherefore did
I marry, but to make lawful prize of a rich widow’s wealth,
and squander it on love and you?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Deceit and frivolous pretense!

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Death, am I not married? What’s pretense? Am I not
imprisoned, fettered? Have I not a wife? Nay a wife that
was a window, a young widow, a handsome widow; and
would be again a widow, but that I have a heart of proof,
and something of a constitution to bustle through the ways of
wedlock and this world. Will you yet be reconciled to truth
and me?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Impossible. Truth and you are inconsistent. I hate you, and
shall for ever.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: For loving you?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
I loathe the name of love after such usage; and next to the
guilt with which you would asperse me, I scorn you most.
Farewell!

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Nay, we must not part thus.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Let me go.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: Come, I’m sorry.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
I care not, let me go. Break my hands, do! I’d leave ’em
to get loose.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
I would not hurt you for the world. Have I no other hold to
keep you here?

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Well, I have deserved it all.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: You know I love you.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: Poor dissembling! Oh, that —Well, it is not yet—

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
What? what is it not? What is it not yet? It is not yet too
late—

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: No, it is not yet too late; I have that comfort.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p: It is, to love another.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
But not to loathe, detest, abhor mankind, myself, and the
whole treacherous world.

sp.speaker: FAINALL.
sp.p:
Nay, this is extravagance. Come, I ask your pardon. No
tears. I was to blame; I could not love you and be easy in
my doubts. Pray, forbear. I believe you. I’m convinced I’ve
done you wrong; and any way, every way will make amends.
I’ll hate my wife yet more, damn her! I’ll part with her, rob
her of all she’s worth, and we’ll retire somewhere, anywhere,
to another world. I’ll marry thee; be pacified. ’Sdeath, they
come; hide your face, your tears. You have a mask; wear it
a moment. This way, this way. Be persuaded.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: They are here yet.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: They are turning into the other walk.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
While I only hated my husband, I could bear to see him;
but since I have despised him, he’s too offensive.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Oh, you should hate with prudence.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Yes, for I have loved with indiscretion.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You should have just so much disgust for your husband as
may be sufficient to make you relish your lover.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
You have been the cause that I hate loved without bounds,
and would you set limits to that aversion of which you have
been the occasion? Why did you make me marry this man?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Why do we daily commit disagreeable and dangerous
actions? To save that idol, reputation. If the familiarities
of our loves had produced that consequence of which you
were apprehensive, where could you have fixed a father’s
name with credit, but on a husband? I knew Fainall to be a
man lavish of his morals, an interested and professing friend,
a false and a designing lover; yet one whose wit and outward
fair behavior have gained a reputation with the town enough
to make that woman stand excused who has suffered herself
to be won by his addresses. A better man ought not to have
been sacrificed to the occasion; a worse had not answered to
the purpose. When you are weary of him, you know your
remedy.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
I ought to stand in some degree of credit with you,
Mirabell.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
In justice to you, I have made you privy to my whole design,
and put it in your power to ruin or advance my fortune.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Whom have you instructed to represent your pretended
uncle?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Waitwell, my servant.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
He is humble servant to Foible, my mother’s woman,
and may win her to your interest.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Care is taken for that. She is won and worn by this time.
They were married this morning.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Waitwell and Foible. I would not tempt my servant to
betray me by trusting him too far. If your mother, in
hopes to ruin me, should consent to marry my pretended
uncle, he might, like Mosca in The Fox, stand upon terms;
so I made him sure beforehand.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
So, if my poor mother is caught in a contract, you will
discover the imposture betimes, and release her by producing
a certificate of her gallant’s former marriage.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Yes, upon condition she consent to my marriage with her
niece, and surrender the moiety of her fortune in her
possession.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
She talked last night of endeavoring at a match between
Millamant and your uncle.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
That was by Foible’s direction, and my instruction, that
she might seem to carry it more privately.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Well, I have an opinion of your success, for I believe my
lady will do anything to get a husband; and when she has
this, which you have provided for her, I suppose she will
submit to anything to get rid of him.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Yes, I think the good lady would marry anything that
resembled a man, though ’twere no more than a butler
could pinch out of a napkin.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Female frailty! We must all come to it, if we live to be old
and feel the craving of a false appetite when the true is
decayed.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
An old woman’s appetite is depraved like that of a girl.
’Tis the green sickness of a second childhood; and like the
faint offer of a latter spring, serves but to usher in the fall,
and withers in an affected bloom.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Here’s your mistress.

div1.stage: Enter Mrs. Millamant, Witwoud, and Mincing.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Here she comes, i’faith, full sail, with her fan spread and
her streamers out, and a shoal of fools for tenders. Ha,
no, I cry her mercy!

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
I see but one poor empty sculler; and he tows her woman
after him.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You seem to be unattended, madam. You used to have the
beau monde throng after you, and a flock of gay fine perukes
hovering round you.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Like moths about a candle. I had like to have lost my
comparison for want of breath.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Oh, I have denied myself airs today. I have walked as fast
through the crowd—

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: As a favorite in disgrace, and with as few followers.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Dear Mr. Witwoud, truce with your similitudes; for I am
as sick of ’em—

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
As a physician of a good air. I cannot help it, madam,
though ’tis against myself.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: Yet again! Mincing, stand between me and his wit.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Do, Mrs. Mincing, like a screen before a great fire. I
confess I do blaze today; I am too bright.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: But, dear Millamant, why were you so long?

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Long! Lord, have I not made violent haste? I have asked
every living thing I met for you; I have inquired after
you, as after a new fashion.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Madam, truce with your similitudes. No, you met her
husband, and did not ask him for her.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
By your leave, Witwoud, that were like inquiring after an
old fashion, to ask a husband for his wife.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: Hum, a hit! a hit! a palpable hit! I confess it.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: You were dressed before I came abroad.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Aye, that’s true. Oh, but then I had—Mincing, what had
I? Why was I so long?

sp.speaker: MINCING.
sp.p: O mem, your la’ship stayed to peruse a pecquet of letters.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Oh, aye, letters; I had letters. I am persecuted with letters.
I hate letters. Nobody knows how to write letters; and yet
one has ’em, one does not know why. They serve one to pin
up one’s hair.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Is that the way? Pray, madam, do you pin up your hair with
all your letters? I find I must keep copies.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Only with those in verse, Mr. Witwoud. I never pin up my
hair with prose. I fancy one’s hair would not curl if it were
pinned up with prose. I think I tried once, Mincing.

sp.speaker: MINCING.
sp.p: O mem, I shall never forget it.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: Aye, poor Mincing tift and tift all the morning.

sp.speaker: MINCING.
sp.p:
’Till I had the cremp in my fingers, I’ll vow, mem. And
all to no purpose. But when your la’ship pins it up with
poetry, it sits so pleasant the next day as anything, and is so
pure and so crips.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p: Indeed, so crips?

sp.speaker: MINCING.
sp.p: You’re such a critic, Mr. Witwoud.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Mirabell, did not you take exceptions last night? Oh, aye,
and went away. Now I think on’t, I’m angry. No, now I
think on’t, I’m pleased; for I believe I gave you some pain.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Does that please you?

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: Infinitely; I love to give pain.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You would affect a cruelty which is not in your nature;
your true vanity is in the power of pleasing.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Oh, I ask your pardon for that. One’s cruelty is one’s power;
and when one parts with one’s cruelty, one parts with
one’s power; and when one has parted with that, I fancy
one’s old and ugly.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Aye, aye, suffer your cruelty to ruin the object of your
power, to destroy your lover, and then how vain, how lost
a thing you’ll be! Nay, ’tis true: you are no longer handsome
when you’ve lost your lover; your beauty dies upon the
instant. For beauty is the lover’s gift; ’tis he bestows your
charms, your glass is all a cheat. The ugly and the old, whom
the looking glass mortifies, yet after commendation can be
flattered by it, and discover beauties in it; for that reflects
our praises, rather than your face.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Oh, the vanity of these men! Fainall, d’ye hear him? If
they did not commend us, we were not handsome! Now you
must know they could not commend one, if one was not
handsome. Beauty the lover’s gift! Lord, what is a lover,
that it can give? Why, one makes lovers as fast as one pleases,
and they live as long as one pleases, and they die as soon as
one pleases; and then, if one pleases, one makes more.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
Very pretty. Why, you make no more of making of lovers,
madam, than of making so many card-matches.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
One no more owes one’s beauty to a lover than one’s wit to
an echo. They can but reflect what we look and say; vain
empty things if we are silent or unseen, and want a being.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Yet to those two vain empty things you owe two [of] the
greatest pleasures of your life.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
To your lover you owe the pleasure of hearing yourselves
praised; and to an echo the pleasure of hearing yourselves
talk.

sp.speaker: WITWOUD.
sp.p:
But I know a lady that loves talking so incessantly, she won’t
give an echo fair play; she has that everlasting rotation of
tongue, that an echo must wait till she dies, before it can
catch her last words.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: Oh, fiction! Fainall, let us leave these men.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Immediately. I have a word or two for Mr. Witwoud.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I would beg a little private audience too. You had the
tyranny to deny me last night, though you knew I came to
impart a secret to you that concerned my love.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: You saw I was engaged.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Unkind! You had the leisure to entertain a herd of fools;
things who visit you from their excessive idleness, bestowing
on your easiness that time which is the incumbrance of
their lives. How can you find delight in such society? It is
impossible they should admire you; they are not capable.
Or if they were, it should be to you as a mortification, for
sure to please a fool is some degree of folly.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
I please myself. Besides, sometimes to converse with fools
is for my health.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You health! Is there a worse disease than the conversation
of fools?

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: Yes, the vapors; fools are physic for it, next to assafoetida.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: You are not in a course of fools?

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Mirabell, if you persist in this offensive freedom, you’ll
displeased me. I think I must resolve, after all, not to have
you; we shan’t agree.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Not in our physic, it may be.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
And yet our distemper, in all likelihood, will be the same;
for we shall be sick of one another. I shan’t endure to be
reprimanded nor instructed; ’tis so dull to act always by
advice, and so tedious to be told of one’s faults—I can’t bear
it. Well, I won’t have you, Mirabell—I’m resolved—I think
—you may go. —Ha! ha! ha! What would you give that you
could help loving me?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I would give something that you did not know I could not
help it.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p: Come, don’t look grave then. Well, what do you say to me?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I say that a man may as soon make a friend by his wit, or a
fortune by his honesty, as win a woman with plain dealing
and sincerity.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Sententious Mirabell! Prithee, don’t look with that violent
and inflexible wise face, like Solomon at the dividing of the
child in an old tapestry hanging.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
You are merry, madam, but I would persuade you for one
moment to be serious.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
What, with that face? No, if you keep your countenance,
’tis impossible I should hold mine. Well, after all, there is
something very moving in a love-sick face. Ha! ha! ha!
—Well, I won’t laugh, don’t be peevish—Heighho! Now I’ll
be melancholy, as melancholy as a watch-light. Well, Mirabell,
if ever you will win me, woo me now. —Nay, if you are
so tedious, fare you well. —I see they are walking away.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Can you not find in the variety of your disposition one
moment—

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
To hear you tell me Foible’s married, and your plot like
to speed? —No.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: But how came you to know it?

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Unless by the help of the devil, you can’t imagine; unless
she should tell me herself. Which of the two it may have
been, I will leave you to consider; and when you have done
thinking of that, think of me.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
I have something more—Gone! Think of you! To think of
a whirlwind, though ’twere in a whirlwind, were a case of
more steady contemplation; a very tranquility of mind and
mansion. A fellow that lives in a windmill has not a more
whimsical dwelling than the heart of a man that is lodged
in a woman. There is no point of the compass to which
they cannot turn, and by which they are not turned; and
by one as well as another, for motion, not method, is their
occupation. To know this, and yet continue to be in love, is
to be made wise from the dictates of reason, and yet per-
severe to play the fool by the force of instinct. —Oh, here
come my pair of turtles! —What, billing so sweetly! Is not
Valentine’s Day over with you yet? Enter Waitwell and Foible.
Sirrah, Waitwell, why sure you think you were married for
your own recreation, and not for my conveniency.

sp.speaker: WAITWELL.
sp.p:
Your pardon, sir. With submission, we have indeed been
solacing in lawful delights; but still with an eye to business,
sir. I have instructed her as well as I could. If she can
take your directions as readily as my instructions, sir, your
affairs are in a prosperous way.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Give you joy, Mrs. Foible.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
O las, sir, I’m so ashamed! I’m afraid my lady has been in a
thousand inquietudes for me. But I protest, sir, I made as
much haste as I could.

sp.speaker: WAITWELL.
sp.p:
That she did indeed, sir. It was my fault that she did not
make more.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: That I believe.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
But I told my lady as you instructed me, sir, that I had a
prospect of seeing Sir Rowland, your uncle; and that I would
put her ladyship’s picture in my pocket to show him, which
I’ll be sure to say has made him so enamored of her beauty,
that he burns with impatience to lie at her ladyship’s feet and
worship the original.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Excellent Foible! Matrimony has made you eloquent in
love.

sp.speaker: WAITWELL.
sp.p: I think she has profited, sir. I think so.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p: You have seen Madam Millamant, sir?

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
I told her, sir, because I did not know that you might find
an opportunity; she had so much company last night.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p: Your diligence will merit more. In the meantime—

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p: O dear sir, your humble servant.

sp.speaker: WAITWELL.
sp.p: Spouse.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Stand off, sir, not a penny! Go on and prosper, Foible; the
lease shall be made good and the farm stocked, if we
succeed.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
I don’t question your generosity, sir; and you need not
doubt of success. If you have no more commands, sir,
I’ll be gone; I’m sure my lady is at her toilet and can’t dress
till I come. —Oh dear, I’m sure that ( looking out) was
Mrs. Marwood that went by in a mask; if she has seen me
with you I’m sure she’ll tell my lady. I’ll make haste
home and prevent her. Your servant, sir. B’w’y, Waitwell.

sp.speaker: WAITWELL.
sp.p:
Sir Rowland, if you please. The jade’s so pert upon her
preferment she forgets herself.

sp.speaker: MIRABELL.
sp.p:
Come, sir, will you endeavor to forget yourself, and trans-
form into Sir Rowland?

sp.speaker: WAITWELL.
sp.p:
Why, sir, it will be impossible I should remember myself.
Married, knighted, and attended all in one day! ’Tis enough
to make any man forget himself. The difficulty will be how to
recover my acquaintance and familiarity with my former self,
and fall from my transformation to a reformation into
Waitwell. Nay, I shan’t be quite the same Waitwell neither;
for now I remember me, I am married and can’t be my own
man again.

lg.l: Aye, there’s the grief; that’s the sad change of life,
To lose my title, and yet keep my wife.

div1.head: [III]
div1.stage: A Room in Lady Wishfort’s House.
Lady Wishfort at her toilet, Peg waiting.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p: Merciful! no news of Foible yet?

sp.speaker: PEG.
sp.p: No, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
I have no more patience. If I have not fretted myself till I
am pale again, there’s no veracity in me! Fetch me the
red; the red, do you hear, sweetheart? An arrant ash-
color, as I’m a person! Look you how this wench stirs! Why
dost thou not fetch me a little red? Didst thou not hear me,
mopus?

sp.speaker: PEG.
sp.p:
The red ratafia does your ladyship mean, or the cherry
brandy?

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Ratafia, fool! No, fool! Not the ratafia, fool. Grant me
patience! I mean the Spanish paper, idiot; complexion,
darling. Paint, paint, paint, dost thou understand that,
changeling, dangling thy hands like bobbins before thee?
Why dost thou not stir, puppet? thou wooden thing upon
wires!

sp.speaker: PEG.
sp.p:
Lord, madam, your ladyship is so impatient! I cannot
come at the paint, madam; Mrs. Foible has locked it up
and carried the key with her.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
A pox take you both! Fetch me the cherry brandy then. (Exit Peg.)
I’m as pale and as faint, I look like Mrs.
Qualmsick, the curate’s wife, that’s always breeding.
Wench, come, come, wench, what art thou doing? sipping?
tasting? Save thee, dost thou not know the bottle?

div1.stage: Re-enter Peg with a bottle and china cup.

sp.speaker: PEG.
sp.p: Madam, I was looking for a cup.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
A cup, save thee! and what a cup hast thou brought!
Dost thou take me for a fairy, to drink out of an acorn?
Why didst thou not bring thy thimble? Hast thou ne’er a
brass thimble clinking in thy pocket with a bit of nutmeg?
I warrant thee. Come, fill, fill! So; again. (One knocks.)
See who that is. Set down the bottle first. Here, here, under
the table. What, wouldst thou go with the bottle in thy
hand, like a tapster? As I’m a person, this wench has
lived in an inn upon the road, before she came to me,
like Maritornes the Asturian in Don Quixote! No Foible yet?

sp.speaker: PEG.
sp.p: No, madam, Mrs. Marwood.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p: Oh, Marwood, let her come in. Come in, good Marwood.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
I’m surprised to find your ladyship in dishabillé at this
time of day.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Foible’s a lost thing; has been abroad since morning, and
never heard of since.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
I saw her but now, as I came masked through the park, in
conference with Mirabell.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
With Mirabell! You call my blood into my face with
mentioning that traitor. She durst not have the confidence!
I sent her to negotiate an affair in which, if I’m detected, I’m
undone. If that wheedling villain has wrought upon Foible
to detect me, I’m ruined. Oh my dear friend, I’m a wretch
of wretches if I’m detected.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: O madam, you cannot suspect Mrs. Foible’s integrity.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Oh, he carries poison in his tongue that would corrupt
integrity itself! If she has given him an opportunity, she has
as good as put her integrity into his hands. Ah, dear
Marwood, what’s integrity to an opportunity? Hark! I hear
her! Go, you thing, and send her in. (Exit Peg.)
Dear friend, retire into my closet, that I may examine her with
more freedom. You’ll pardon me, dear friend; I can make
bold with you. There are books over the chimney. Quarles
and Prynne, and the Short View of the Stage, with Bunyan’s
works, to entertain you. Exit Mrs. Marwood. Enter Foible.
O Foible, where hast thou been? What hast thou been
doing?

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p: Madam, I have seen the party.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p: But what hast thou done?

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
Nay, ’tis your ladyship has done, and are to do; I have
only promised. But a man so enamored, so transported!
Well, here it is, all that is left; all that is not kissed away.
Well, if worshiping of pictures be a sin, poor Sir Rowland,
I say.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
The miniature has been counted like. But hast thou not
betrayed me, Foible? Hast thou not detected me to that
faithless Mirabell? What hadst thou to do with him in the
Park? Answer me, has he got nothing out of thee?

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
[aside] So the devil has been beforehand with me. What shall I say?
—Alas, madam, could I help it, if I met that confident
thing? Was I in fault? If you had heard how he used me,
and all upon your ladyship’s account, I’m sure you would
not suspect my fidelity. Nay, if that had been the worst, I
could have borne; but he had a fling at your ladyship too.
And then I could not hold; but i’faith I gave him his own.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p: Me? What did the filthy fellow say?

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
O madam! ’tis a shame to say what he said, with his taunts
and his fleers, tossing up his nose. Humph! (says he), what,
you are a hatching some plot (says he), you are so early
abroad, or catering (say he), ferreting for some disbanded
officer, I warrant. Half-pay is but thin subsistence (says he).
Well, what pension does your lady propose? Let me see
(says he), what, she must come down pretty deep now, she’s
superannuated (says he) and—

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Ods my life, I’ll have him, I’ll have him murdered. I’ll have
him poisoned. Where does he eat? I’ll marry a drawer to
have him poisoned in his wine. I’ll send for Robin from
Locket’s immediately.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
Poison him? Poisoning’s too good for him. Starve him,
madam, starve him; marry Sir Rowland and get him
disinherited. Oh, you would bless yourself to hear what he
said!

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p: A villain! superannuated!

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
Humph! (says he), I hear you are laying designs against
me too (says he), and Mrs. Millamant is to marry my uncle
(he does not suspect a word of your ladyship); but (says he)
I’ll fit you for that. I warrant you (says he), I’ll hamper you
for that (says he), you and your old frippery too (says he),
I’ll handle you—

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Audacious villain! Handle me! would he durst! Frippery?
old frippery! Was there ever such a foulmouthed fellow?
I’ll be married tomorrow; I’ll be contracted tonight.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p: The sooner the better, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p: Will Sir Rowland be here, say’st thou? When, Foible?

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
Incontinently, madam. No new sheriff’s wife expects the
return of her husband after knighthood with that impatience
in which Sir Rowland burns for the dear hour of kissing
your ladyship’s hands after dinner.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Frippery? superannuated frippery! I’ll frippery the villain;
I’ll reduce him to frippery and rags! A tatterdemalion! I
hope to see him hung with tatters, like a Long Lane penthouse
or a gibbet thief. A slander-mouthed railer! I
warrant the spendthrift prodigal’s in debt as much as the
million lottery, or the whole court upon a birthday. I’ll
spoil his credit with his tailor. Yes, he shall have my niece
with her fortune, he shall!

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
He! I hope to see him lodge in Ludgate first, and angle
into Blackfairs for brass farthings with an old mitten.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Aye, dear Foible; thank thee for that, dear Foible. He has
put me out of all patience. I shall never recompose my
features to receive Sir Rowland with any economy of face.
This wretch has fretted me that I am absolutely decayed.
Look, Foible.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
Your ladyship has frowned a little too rashly, indeed,
madam. There are some cracks discernible in the white
varnish.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Let me see the glass. Cracks, say’st thou? Why I am
arrantly flayed; I look like an old peeled wall. Thou must
repair me, Foible, before Sir Rowland comes, or I shall
never keep up to my picture.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
I warrant you, madam, a little art once made your picture
like you; and now a little of the same art must make you
like your picture. Your picture must sit for you, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
But art thou sure Sir Rowland will not fail to come? Or
will he not fail when he does come? Will he be importunate,
Foible, and push? For if he should not be importunate, I
shall never break decorums. I shall die with confusion, if I
am forced to advance. Oh no, I can never advance! I shall
swoon if he should expect advances. No, I hope Sir Rowland
is better bred than to put a lady to the necessity of
breaking her forms. I won’t be too coy neither. I won’t give
him despair; but a little disdain is not amiss, a little scorn is
alluring.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p: A little scorn becomes your ladyship.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Yes, but tenderness becomes me best, a sort of a dyingness.
You see that picture has a sort of a—ha, Foible? a swimmingness
in the eyes. Yes, I’ll look so. My niece affects it;
but she wants features. Is Sir Rowland handsome? Let my
toilet be removed. I’ll dress above. I’ll receive Sir Rowland
here. Is he handsome? Don’t answer me. I won’t know; I’ll
be surprised, I’ll be taken by surprise.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p: By storm, madam. Sir Rowland’s a brisk man.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Is he! Oh, then he’ll importune, if he’s a brisk man.
I shall save decorums if Sir Rowland importunes. I have
a mortal terror at the apprehension of offending against
decorums. Nothing but importunity can surmount decorums.
Oh, I’m glad he’s a brisk man. Let my things be removed,
good Foible.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
O Foible, I have been in a fright, lest I should come too
late! That devil Marwood saw you in the Park with Mirabell,
and I’m afraid will discover it to my lady.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p: Discover what, madam?

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p:
Nay, nay, put not on that strange face. I am privy to the
whole design, and know that Waitwell, to whom thou wert
this morning married, is to personate Mirabell’s uncle, and
as such, winning my lady, to involve her in those difficulties
from which Mirabell only must release her, by his making
his conditions to have my cousin and her fortune left to her
own disposal.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
O dear madam, I beg your pardon. It was not my confidence
in your ladyship that was deficient; but I thought the former
good correspondence between your ladyship and Mr. Mirabell
might have hindered his communicating this secret.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: Dear Foible, forget that.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
O dear madam, Mr. Mirabell is such a sweet, winning
gentleman, but your ladyship is the pattern of generosity.
Sweet lady, to be so good! Mr. Mirabell cannot choose but
be grateful. I find your ladyship has his heart still. Now,
madam, I can safely tell your ladyship our success. Mrs.
Marwood had told my lady; but I warrant I managed myself.
I turned it all for the better. I told my lady that Mr. Mirabell
railed at her. I laid horrid things to his charge, I’ll vow;
and my lady is so incensed that she’ll be contracted to Sir
Rowland tonight, she says. I warrant I worked her up, that
he may have her for asking for, as they say of a Welsh
maidenhead.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: O rare Foible!

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
Madam, I beg your ladyship to acquaint Mr. Mirabell of
his success. I would be seen as little as possible to speak to
him; besides, I believe Madame Marwood watches me.
She has a month’s mind; but I know Mr. Mirabell can’t
abide her. ( Enter Footman.) John, remove my lady’s
toilet. Madam, your servant. My lady is so impatient,
I fear she’ll come for me, if I stay.

sp.speaker: MRS. FAINALL.
sp.p: I’ll go with you up the backstairs, lest I should meet her.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Indeed, Mrs. Engine, is it thus with you? Are you become a
go-between of this importance? Yes, I shall watch you. Why
this wench is the passe-partout, a very master key to everybody’s
strongbox. My friend Fainall, have you carried it so
swimmingly? I thought there was something in it; but it
seems it’s over with you. Your loathing is not from a want of
appetite then, but from a surfeit. Else you could never be so
cool to fall from a principal to be an assistant; to procure
for him! A pattern of generosity, that I confess. Well, Mr.
Fainall, you have met with your match. O man, man!
woman, woman! The devil’s an ass; if I were a painter, I
would draw him like an idiot, a driveler with a bib and
bells. Man should have his head and horns, and woman the
rest of him. Poor simple fiend! Madam Marwood has a
month’s mind, but he can’t abide her. ’Twere better for him
you had not been his confessor in that affair, without you
could have kept his counsel closer. I shall not prove
another pattern of generosity and stalk for him, till he takes
his stand to aim at a fortune. He has not obligated me to that,
with those excesses of himself; and now I’ll have none of
him. Here comes the good lady, panting ripe; with a heart
full of hope, and a head full of care, like any chemist upon
the day of projection.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
O dear Marwood, what shall I say, for this rude forgetfullness?
But my dear friend is all goodness.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
No apologies, dear madam. I have been very well
entertained.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
As I’m a person, I am in a very chaos to think I should so
forget myself; but I have such an olio of affairs, really I know
not what to do. — ( Calls.) Foible! —I expect my nephew,
Sir Wilfull, every moment too. —Why, Foible! —He
means to travel for improvement.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Methinks Sir Wilfull should rather think of marrying than
traveling at his years. I hear he is turned of forty.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Oh, he’s in less danger of being spoiled by his travels. I
am against my nephew’s marrying too young. It will be
time enough when he comes back and has acquired discretion
to choose for himself.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p:
Methinks Mrs. Millamant and he would make a very
fit match. He may travel afterwards. ’Tis a thing very
usual with young gentlemen.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
I promise you I have thought on’t; and since ’tis your
judgment, I’ll think on’t again. I assure you I will; I value
your judgment extremely. On my word, I’ll propose it. Enter Foible.
Come, come, Foible, I had forgot my nephew will be here
before dinner. I must make haste.

sp.speaker: FOIBLE.
sp.p:
Mr. Witwoud and Mr. Petulant are come to dine with your
ladyship.

sp.speaker: LADY WISHFORT.
sp.p:
Oh dear, I can’t appear till I’m dressed. Dear Marwood,
shall I be free with you again, and beg you to entertain ’em?
I’ll make all imaginable haste. Dear friend, excuse me.

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
Sure never anything was so unbred as that odious man!
Marwood, your servant.

sp.speaker: MRS. MARWOOD.
sp.p: You have a color, what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: MILLAMANT.
sp.p:
That horrid fellow, Petulant, has provoked me into a flame.
